name: Elena Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of three doctors at the valley clinic, which covers six farming villages along one long road. Mornings I see patients in the clinic, and after lunch I drive out on home visits in an old four-wheel drive, because half my patients are too old or too far out to come in. I like the visits best: the kitchen tables, the dogs, the cup of tea I'm not supposed to accept. What wears me out is the computer, honestly, and the hour every evening of typing up what I already wrote in my notebook.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You still keep a paper notebook?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Always, a small black one in my coat pocket. I write while I'm in someone's kitchen, then type it up at night, which is twice the work, I know. The clinic manager keeps offering me the AI note-taker, and I keep saying no, thank you. I've never used one of those tools and I'm not in a hurry to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine by me, and I'd mean it. At the clinic I'd say the other two can keep their gadgets. I don't really post online, but I'd tell my partner it sounds about right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays as it is, and that's not exactly comfortable. Jonas is a carpenter working for himself, so some months he earns well and some months nothing. The four-wheel drive is on a loan, we rent the cottage, and if the car breaks down in winter we don't have the money to fix it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the notebook and the home visits. I'd try to put a little aside each month, maybe by taking packed lunches instead of the café in the village. That's about it, because nothing in this picture asks me to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, nervous about the money. Those two have always lived side by side for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned winter and the car. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February the gearbox went halfway up the hill to the Hoffmann farm, and it cost more than I had in the bank. Jonas's brother lent us the money and we paid him back over four months. I don't want to ask him again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at the clinic push you harder on the note-taker in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, but there are only three of us and they need me for the home visits. Nobody else wants to drive those roads in the snow. As long as that's true, I can keep my notebook.

say: That's **fine by her**, and she'd mean it: the others can keep their gadgets.
She'd tell her partner the **hype** picture sounds about right.
think: Life stays the same, and that means **irregular income** from her partner's carpentry.
The **four-wheel drive** is on a loan, and a winter breakdown would empty the bank.
do: Keep using the **paper notebook** and doing afternoon home visits.
Take **packed lunches** instead of the village café to save a little each month.
feel: Calm about the **job**, nervous about the **money**, as always.
S0.quote: Last February the gearbox went halfway up the hill to the Hoffmann farm, and it cost more than I had in the bank.
fieldNote: Her job feels secure because nobody else wants the **snowy home visits**, but money doesn't.
A **gearbox repair** last winter, covered by her partner's brother, still weighs on her.
Her resistance to AI is **quiet and settled**, not angry.

steps.text: Keep the paper notebook and the afternoon home visits
Take packed lunches instead of the village café

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, and that not every patient wants to talk to a computer. At the clinic I'd say it plainly to the manager. I wouldn't make speeches; that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be pushed. If the software does the letters, the test results and the booking, the clinic will expect the three of us to see more people. And the doctor who refuses the tools will look slow next to the other two, which would be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the practice nurse show me the basics of the note-taker, grudgingly, because I'd rather choose to learn than be told to. I'd offer to take on all the home visits, since that's the part a computer can't do. We'd skip our summer week at the lake to keep a bit more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot of worry. I don't like being the one holding things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather choose to learn than be told. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the manager tells me to use the note-taker, it means they've already decided I'm a problem. If I go to the nurse myself, I keep some say in it. It's pride, partly, I admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas say about skipping the lake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble and then agree, because he knows his own work is up and down. He's the one who says we should have more saved, and he's right. It's just never the right month to start.

say: Not every patient wants to **talk to a computer**, and care is needed.
She'd tell the manager **plainly**, without making speeches.
think: The clinic would expect **more patients** once software takes letters and booking.
The doctor refusing the tools would **look slow**, and that's her.
do: Ask the practice nurse to show her the **note-taker basics**, by choice.
Offer to take on **all home visits**, the part a computer can't do.
Skip the summer **week at the lake** to keep more in the bank.
feel: Uneasy, with a **knot of worry** about holding things up.
S1.quote: If the manager tells me to use the note-taker, it means they've already decided I'm a problem.
fieldNote: She'd learn the tool **on her own terms** to avoid being marked as the problem.
Claiming **all the home visits** is her way of making herself necessary.
She admits **pride** plays a part, which she says openly.

steps.text: Ask the practice nurse to teach her the note-taker basics
Take over all of the clinic's afternoon home visits
Skip this summer's week at the lake

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that it's madness, and that someone should slow it down. I'd say it to Jonas over dinner, because I'm not someone who goes on the internet about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't have a plan, I have a car loan. By 2028 the thinking part of the job, which is most of what they pay a doctor for, is done by software. The home visits last until robots come in 2031, but would they pay a doctor to make tea in a kitchen? I doubt it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the frightening part. I'd probably just keep going to work until someone told me otherwise. If it got bad, we'd ask Jonas's parents whether we could live in the flat above their barn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest goes tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep going until someone told you otherwise. Is there nothing you'd do earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I should. But I've spent eleven years training for this one job, and I don't know how to do anything else. Two years isn't long enough to become someone new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your patients on the home visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, at first. Old Mrs Brandt on the hill farm would notice anyway, because she notices everything. She'd probably make me a cup of tea and tell me it'll be fine, which is backwards.

say: It's **madness**, and someone should slow it down.
She doesn't know **what she'd say**, which is unusual for her.
She'd say it to Jonas over dinner, **not online**.
think: She has **no plan**, only a car loan, as software takes most of the job by 2028.
Home visits last until 2031, but she doubts anyone pays a **doctor's wage** for them.
do: Keep **going to work** until someone tells her otherwise.
Ask Jonas's parents about living in the **flat above their barn** if money runs out.
feel: Panicky, with her **chest tightening** just at the thought.
S2.quote: I don't have a plan, I have a car loan.
fieldNote: She's **overwhelmed**: eleven years of training and no idea how to do anything else.
Her only fallback is **family**: the flat above her partner's parents' barn.
The image of a **patient comforting her** shows how upside down this feels.

steps.text: Keep doing her clinic sessions until told otherwise
Ask Jonas's parents about the flat above their barn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast, but at least there's a bit of warning. At the clinic I'd ask the other two what they're planning, because I wouldn't know where to start. I'd keep my voice down about it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could maybe move into palliative care, looking after dying patients at home. Palliative care is kitchens and bedsides, and that's close to what I love. It's hands-on, and it lasts until robots come around 2034, even if it's not exactly what I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the hospice in town if they'd take me for part-time training next year. I'd try to pay down the car loan before then. And I'd stop saying no to the note-taker, because I'd need the evening hours back for study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened. But there's a door, which there wasn't in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you find the time for hospice training with clinic work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop to four days at the clinic and do one day at the hospice, which means less pay for a year. Jonas would have to take every job going. It would be tight, and I'd be tired, but I think we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you still worried you'd lose most of your income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, by 2034 or so, even with the hospice. Palliative care will still change when the robots come. I'd be thirty-five and back where I am now, just older.

She'd **quietly ask** her two colleagues what they're planning.
think: Five years could let her move into **palliative care** at home, which lasts until 2034.
Bedsides and kitchens are **close** to what she loves, if not what she trained for.
do: Ask the town **hospice** about part-time training next year.
Drop to **four days** at the clinic for a year, with less pay.
Pay down the **car loan** before the training starts.
feel: Still **frightened**, but able to see a door.
S3.quote: Palliative care is kitchens and bedsides, and that's close to what I love.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **door** into palliative care that the fast picture didn't.
She'd finally accept the **note-taker** to free up evenings for study.
She still expects to lose **most of her income** by 2034, which keeps her alarmed.

steps.text: Ask the town hospice about part-time palliative training
Drop to four clinic days for a year of training
Pay down the car loan before training starts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and that's enough for most of us to find our feet. At the clinic I'd say we should plan as a team. I'd still be cautious about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years helps me most of all. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes and forty around 2039 when robots come for the visits. By then the car's paid off, I'd have palliative training, and Jonas's carpentry might even be doing better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the car loan in the first two years and start the hospice training in year three. I'd learn the note-taker properly, slowly, since I'd have time. And I'd try to save three months' worth, which would be the first time ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. I learn slowly, but I do learn, and ten years is enough time to get used to an idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you don't know how to do anything else. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Ten years is enough to train properly and get comfortable, which two years isn't. I learn slowly, but I do learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a medical student today in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To find the part of medicine where you have to be in the room. And to keep a little notebook, because you remember things better when you write them by hand.

say: Ten years is **enough** for most people to find their feet.
The clinic should **plan as a team**, and she'd stay cautious in public.
think: Ten years **helps her most**: she'd be thirty-seven when thinking work goes.
By 2039 the car is paid off and she'd have **palliative training**.
do: Pay off the **car loan** in the first two years.
Learn the **note-taker** properly and save three months' worth.
feel: Uneasy rather than **frightened**, with time to get used to the idea.
S4.quote: I learn slowly, but I do learn, and ten years is enough time to get used to an idea.
fieldNote: Time matters most to her because she **learns slowly** and knows it.
Her path is the same as before, **palliative care**, just properly prepared.
She'd still lose the **thinking work** at thirty-seven, so the worry remains.

steps.text: Pay off the four-wheel drive loan in two years
Start part-time hospice training in year three
Learn the clinic's note-taker properly, at her own pace

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing ready and no money to fall back on. What would help is time, really, and some way to train for hands-on work without losing a whole year's pay. A training wage, something like that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the home visits. People think doctors sit behind desks, but half my day is driving up muddy roads to people who can't come to us. Whoever plans all this should ride along with me for one afternoon in January.

headlineQuote: Whoever plans all this should ride along with me for one afternoon in January.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old** doctor at a three-doctor valley clinic serving six farming villages.
She does the **home visits** in an old four-wheel drive and writes notes in a paper notebook.
Her partner **Jonas** is a self-employed carpenter, and the car loan leaves no buffer.
Fast AGI leaves her **panicked**, with no plan and only family to fall back on.
With five or ten years she'd move into **palliative care** at patients' homes.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd have nothing ready and **no money** behind her.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, and a **training wage** so she can learn hands-on work without losing a year's pay.
